title: Publication: The Passionate Pilgrim (1599)
short: An earlier version was printed in The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), ten years before the 1609 Quarto; it is one of the 'dark lady' sonnets.
body: William Jaggard's anthology The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), sold under Shakespeare's name, opened with a version of this poem, alongside Sonnet 144. The 1599 text differs in several lines ('Unskilful' for 'Unlearned', 'I smiling credit' for 'Simply I credit', 'a soothing tongue' for 'in seeming trust', a different couplet). Scholars disagree whether it is an early draft by Shakespeare or a corrupt text. The archive also holds the 1599 version as 'The Passionate Pilgrim: 1'. 'Made of truth' means entirely truthful, but also faithful in love.

title: swears
short: She swears (takes oaths) that she is faithful; Booth notes that a woman who needs to swear to it already invites doubt.
body: 'Swears' implies oath-taking, which in the context of the sequence (cf. Sonnet 152, 'I am perjur'd most') carries ironic weight: oaths in these sonnets are routinely broken. Booth argues that the very fact of her swearing signals that she is not to be believed. 'Truth' here means fidelity as much as honesty, so the line is about sexual faithfulness. The present tense ('swears') suggests a habitual exchange, repeated as part of the couple's routine.

title: untutor'd youth
short: An untaught, naive young man, inexperienced in the world's deceptions.
body: 'Untutored' means untaught, unschooled. The speaker pretends to believe her so that she will think him young and innocent. 'Unlearned in the world's false subtleties' (l. 4) completes the idea: ignorant of the clever tricks and deceits of the world. The 1599 version reads 'Unskilful in the world's false forgeries'. The irony is that he is, in fact, very well schooled in deceit.

title: vainly
short: Foolishly, emptily; also with a hint of vanity, the speaker's self-flattering wish to seem young.
body: 'Vainly' means in vain, uselessly, and foolishly (OED); the sense of personal vanity is also available. The speaker knows his thought is empty, since she 'knows my days are past the best'. Booth notes the circle of thinking and knowing in ll. 5-6: he thinks she thinks him young, though she knows he is not. The doubled verbs of thinking make the self-deception look elaborate and slightly comic.

anchor: my days are past the best
title: my days are past the best
short: My best years are over; the speaker presents himself as no longer young.
body: The self-portrait of an ageing lover recurs in the Sonnets (cf. Sonnets 62 and 73). Shakespeare was in his early to mid thirties when the 1599 version was printed, which seems young now but was well into middle age by Elizabethan reckoning. Biographical critics have tried to date and identify the relationship (A. L. Rowse's claim for Emilia Lanier is widely rejected); most editors treat the persona as a literary construction.

title: Simply ... simple truth
short: 'Simply' = like a simpleton, foolishly (and also plainly); 'simple truth' = plain truth, which is suppressed on both sides.
body: 'Simply I credit her false-speaking tongue' means I believe her as a fool would, pretending to be simple. 'Credit' means believe, trust, with a pun on financial credit. In l. 8 'simple truth' is plain truth (cf. Sonnet 66, 'simple truth miscall'd simplicity'), and it is 'suppressed' on both sides: neither admits what both know. Booth notes the play between the two 'simple' words.

title: unjust
short: Unfaithful, dishonest; 'just' in love means true to one's vows.
body: 'Unjust' in Shakespeare often means dishonest or faithless, especially in sexual relations (OED). The two rhetorical questions of ll. 9-10 ('wherefore', = why) ask why neither partner admits the truth: her infidelity, his age. The 1599 text reads 'says my love that she is young', a different and weaker question. Burrow and Duncan-Jones both gloss 'unjust' as unfaithful. The balanced pair of questions gives the two lovers equal guilt: her infidelity matches his concealment of his age.

title: love's best habit
short: Love's best behaviour (and best clothing) is the appearance of trust; 'habit' means custom and garment.
body: 'Habit' means both a customary practice and a costume or dress (OED); love dresses itself best in a show of trust. 'Seeming trust' is ambiguous: trust that is only apparent, or trust that seems (appears) to be given. The 'O!' marks the move into general maxim; Vendler reads it as the beginning of proverbial wisdom. The 1599 version has the simpler 'a soothing tongue'.

anchor: loves not to have years told
title: years told
short: Old age, when in love, does not like its years to be counted or spoken of.
body: 'Told' means counted (as in 'telling' money or beads) and also spoken. 'Age in love' is an older person in love, who does not want the count of his years mentioned. The line is proverbial in tone, balancing l. 11. Booth notes the double sense of 'told', linking counting to the speech and lies of the poem. The maxim matches l. 11, and together the two lines generalize the couple's private bargain into a rule about love.

title: I lie with her, and she with me
short: The central pun: they tell lies to each other, and they go to bed together.
body: 'Lie with' means both to lie to and to have sexual intercourse with. The couplet makes the mutual lying the basis of the sexual relationship, the most obvious and best-known pun in the poem. The 1599 text reads 'Therefore I'll lie with love, and love with me', more general and less pointed. Critics disagree on tone: some find the couplet wry and comic, others bitter and self-lacerating (Booth stresses its cynicism; Vendler sees accommodation).

title: in our faults by lies we flatter'd be
short: In our faults (his age, her infidelity) we are comforted and pleased by lies.
body: 'Flatter'd' means soothed, gratified, deceived with pleasing falsehoods (OED). 'Faults' are their failings, but also, sexually, lapses or falls. The 1599 couplet ends 'Since that our faults in love thus smother'd be', so the 1609 text makes flattery, not concealment, the result. Duncan-Jones notes the pun on 'lies' and sexual lying continued from l. 13. The final word 'be' leaves the state open-ended: the lovers remain in mutual flattery rather than reaching any resolution.

title: Structure: questions, maxims, couplet
short: A Shakespearean sonnet of three quatrains and a couplet: two quatrains of mutual deception, a quatrain of questions and maxims, and a punning conclusion.
body: The argument is closely structured: ll. 1-8 set out the deception (she lies about fidelity, he pretends to believe so as to seem young); ll. 9-10 ask two parallel questions beginning 'wherefore'; ll. 11-12 answer with two proverbial maxims; the couplet ('Therefore') concludes logically, as if from a syllogism. Vendler stresses this progression from complaint to acceptance. The pattern of question and answer is clearer in the 1609 version than in 1599.
